intervention.description: Exposure to heavy ion irradiation to assess material behavior

structure.description: Grain refinement

evidence_spans: Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system.

intervention.description: Exposure to dual-beam irradiation combined with helium implantation

structure.description: Low defect generation and evolution with no detectable grain growth

evidence_units.mechanism: Resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation results in low defect generation and evolution
evidence_spans: We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth.

intervention.description: heavy ion irradiation and He implantation

structure.description: no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries
defects: no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: enhanced response to loop formation and He implantation
evidence_spans: Recently, a novel set of alloys based on equiatomic compositions of several principal elements (multi-principal elements alloys (MPEAs) or high-entropy alloys (HEA)) have been developed [16] , [17] . The configurational entropy of mixing in multicomponent alloys tends to be the major thermodynamic driving force to stabilize the solid solution based on simple underlying face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) crystalline structures [18] . Equiatomic compositions maximize the entropic term of the Gibbs free energy of mixing, promoting the formation of random solutions versus intermetallic phases or phase decomposition [19] .
limitations: demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement

material.name: W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf quinary RHEA thin film
material.initial_state: as-deposited nanocrystalline with 24.5 ± 1.3 nm grain size

intervention.description: Heating to increase thermal stability and observe microstructural evolution

structure.description: Single-phase RHEA with slightly increased grain size

evidence_units.mechanism: Thermal activation leading to grain growth in a stable single-phase BCC structure

conditions.environment: TEM vacuum (implied by in situ TEM)

evidence_spans: The average grain size of the as-deposited sample was 24.5 ± 1.3 nm. After annealing to 1173 K for ~30 mins in the TEM, the grain size increased to 26.3 ± 1.1 nm.

The morphology of the as-deposited, and after in situ TEM annealing of the thin film at 1173 K are shown in Fig. 1 a, b , respectively. A single-phase RHEA is clearly shown in the corresponding diffraction patterns.

intervention.description: Ion irradiation to maximize swelling and compare with other W-based materials

structure.description: Nanocrystalline structure with bubbles, no dislocation loops detected

evidence_units.mechanism: Helium implantation leading to bubble formation and grain growth without loop nucleation
evidence_spans: After He implantation, the grain size further increased to 36.3 ± 1.8 nm.
The insets in c , d show underfocused micrographs featuring bubbles.
Dislocation loops were not detected even after 8.5 dpa and at 9.13% He implantation during the dual-beam experiment

intervention.description: Heavy ion damage with He gas production to simulate reactor-relevant conditions

structure.description: Refined nanocrystalline structure with saturation of cavities and lattice strain, no dislocation loops
phases: unknown low phase fraction phase (shallow surface oxides?)

evidence_units.mechanism: Synergistic effect of heavy ion ballistic mixing and He implantation causing grain refinement and cavity saturation
evidence_spans: However, during the dual-beam irradiation, grain refinement occurred, and the average grain size dropped to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after a total irradiation time of ~94 mins.
Thickening of the BCC rings as shown in Fig. 1 g, h indicates the presence of lattice strain, possibly due to defect formation and concentration gradients.

Dislocation loops were not detected even after 8.5 dpa and at 9.13% He implantation during the dual-beam experiment (Supplementary Movie 1 is attached to the supplementary material). Only cavities were observed.
No increasing trends in cavity volume, density, or change in volume occur after that, and saturation is evident for these dpa/He percentage ranges.

intervention.description: High-energy Ar implantation to induce lattice distortion and defect formation

structure.description: Single-phase BCC structure with grain refinement and lattice distortion

evidence_units.mechanism: Synergistic combination of Ar implantation, lattice distortion caused by irradiation ballistic mixing, and grain refinement leading to hardening
evidence_spans: This specimen had a composition of W 31 Ta 34 Cr 5.0 V 27 Hf 3.0 and was irradiated with 400 keV Ar +2 ions at 1073 K to 10 dpa.
The average hardness of the unirradiated sample was measured to be 13.25 GPa.
after irradiation the sample hardness reached a value of 20 GPa.

Increase in hardness after annealing is solely associated with Hf segregation along the GBs whereas the increase after irradiation is a synergistic combination between Ar implantation, lattice distortion caused by irradiation ballistic mixing, and grain refinement.

intervention.description: Observation of elemental segregation at grain boundaries

structure.description: Single-phase BCC with Hf segregation to grain boundaries and inhomogeneous V/Cr distribution

evidence_units.mechanism: Thermal segregation of refractory elements (Hf) to grain boundaries and V/Cr inhomogeneity
evidence_spans: Careful analysis of the elemental maps revealed that after annealing, Hf segregates to grain boundaries, and V and Cr are also inhomogeneously distributed throughout the sample, thus indicating segregation.

intervention.description: He implantation with ~8.45 at.% He

structure.description: nano-crystallinity preserved with grain size increase

evidence_units.mechanism: grain coarsening driven by He implantation without cascade-induced fragmentation
evidence_spans: Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation.
However, grain refinement was not observed for the He only case, but rather grain growth occurred as shown in Fig. 3 .
limitations: grain growth observed during He implantation, though nano-crystallinity preserved

intervention.description: Ar implantation at 1073 K

structure.description: homogenization of elements with no precipitation; striations persist in unirradiated heated part but Hf and Cr lose correlation
microstructure: striations (W-Ta layer and Cr-V-Hf layer) in unirradiated heated part

evidence_units.mechanism: irradiation-induced ballistic mixing and atomic displacement leading to homogenization near the order-disorder transition temperature (ODTT)
evidence_spans: The APT needle extracted from the irradiated sample contained two parts: deep unirradiated, but heated to 1073 K and an irradiated part at 1073 K.
The compositional striations were shown to persist in the heated and unirradiated part, but Hf and Cr have lost their correlation which is predicted by the SRO first-order transition (Fig. 6 ).
The irradiated part showed homogenization of the elements and no precipitation.
This is unlike the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA where irradiation led to uniform and dense Cr-V precipitation [22] .
limitations: Challenging to perform APT on in situ irradiated thin films

intervention.description: Ar implantation at 1073 K

structure.description: no precipitation in irradiated part; homogenized chemical distribution

evidence_units.mechanism: ballistic mixing and atomic displacement causing homogenization when SRO values tend to zero at the ODTT
evidence_spans: The irradiated part showed homogenization of the elements and no precipitation.
This is unlike the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA where irradiation led to uniform and dense Cr-V precipitation [22] .

intervention.description: Ar implantation at 1073 K

structure.description: homogenized chemical distribution

evidence_units.mechanism: ballistic mixing and atomic displacement causing homogenization when SRO values tend to zero
evidence_spans: After irradiation, the hardness further increased by 3.75 GPa.
The 3.75 GPa difference at 200 nm depth can also be explained by Ar implantation as calculated per SRIM, shown in the inset plot of Fig. 5
limitations: synergistic effects of Ar implantation, lattice distortion, and grain refinement

intervention.description: dual-beam irradiation at 1173 K

structure.description: no precipitation observed

evidence_units.mechanism: ODTT of ~1080 K is lower than irradiation temperature of 1173 K, preventing precipitation

comparison.baseline_value: density and size of Cr-V precipitation predicted

evidence_spans: For the in situ irradiated samples, TEM images, and EDX showed no spherical precipitates and for that composition (W 29.4 Ta 42 Cr 5.0 V 16.1 Hf 7.5 ), the SRO and the corresponding atomic configurations (Figs. 6 and 7 ) showed a slightly smaller (1080 K) ODTT (but rather different behavior at lower temperatures) and, therefore, no precipitation is expected during irradiation at 1173 K.

intervention.description: dual-beam irradiation with heavy ions

structure.description: grain refinement via fragmentation of grains into sub-grains

evidence_units.mechanism: cascade effect from heavy ions larger than grain size breaking grains into separate crystalline structures
evidence_spans: One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation.
This suggests that such a grain refinement observed in the dual-beam irradiation case was caused by a cascade effect.
Figure 8 shows grain fragmentation that occurred during the dual-beam irradiation.
Molecular dynamics simulations have shown that high-energy (50 keV) recoil events begin to divide in sub-cascades [34] , [35] , each with a diameter on the order of 10 nm.

This upper limit on cascade size is near the initial grain-size of the W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA, allowing fragmentation to take place whereas, in coarser-grained materials, a similar event would likely result in defect migration to boundaries.
limitations: Fragmentation occurring at faster time scales than frame rate

intervention.description: He implantation to 8.45 dpa and ~8.45 at.%, dual-beam irradiation

structure.description: no dislocation loop formation, negligible volume change, no preferential bubble formation on grain boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: high interstitial-vacancy recombination and lattice distortion limiting defect clustering
evidence_spans: The ion irradiation response of this alloy is characterized by: (1) no dislocation loop formation, (2) negligible change in overall volume due to bubble formation, (3) no preferential bubble formation on grain boundaries despite the high atomic percentage of He implantation at 1173 K, (4) thermally stable grain-size (with 10 nm increase during He implantation up to 8.45% and grain refinement under dual-beam ion irradiation), and (5) no precipitation when used at reactor-relevant temperature (due to intermediate ODTT values).

Pure W, for example, suffers from the formation of large facetted bubbles on the grain matrices and preferential bubble formation with larger sizes on the grain boundaries when implanted with similar He energy but at an even lower implantation value (6.3%) [38] .
The current alloy presents no loop formation and the total change in volume is ~0.3 % after 8.45 dpa and higher percentage of implanted He.
Additionally, no preferential large and facetted cavity formation at the grain boundaries was observed.

intervention.description: annealing treatment

structure.description: Hf segregation to grain boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: Hf segregation to grain boundaries during annealing
evidence_spans: The as-deposited sample had a hardness of 13.25 GPa.
The increase in hardness after annealing was ~3 GPa and this can be directly attributed to Hf segregation to grain boundaries as revealed in Fig. 2 and in the STEM-EDX mapping as insets in Fig. 5 .

intervention.description: Annealed in situ within the TEM

structure.description: post annealed state

outcome.measurement_method: energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy and selected area diffraction (SAED)

evidence_spans: The material was then annealed in situ within the TEM at 1173 K for 10 minutes. EDX and SAED were performed on the thin film sample in the as-deposited and post annealed, implanted, and irradiated conditions.

intervention.description: Irradiated with 400 keV Ar +2 ions

structure.description: post-irradiated state

outcome.property: atomic probe tomography (APT) analysis sample preparation

conditions.environment: Ion Beam Materials Laboratory at Los Alamos National Laboratory

evidence_spans: The ex situ ion irradiations were performed with 400 keV Ar +2 ions on a 200 kV Danfysik Research Ion Implanter at the Ion Beam Materials Laboratory at Los Alamos National Laboratory. The beam flux and the fluence were 1.8 × 10 12 ions/cm 2 /s and 8.2 × 10 15 ions/cm 2 (10 dpa), respectively. The sample was mounted on a heating stage with silver paste and the stage temperature was kept at 1073 K during the irradiation and monitored continuously with a thermocouple mechanically attached to the heating stage. The ex situ irradiation beam parameters were chosen to match the damage process of the in situ irradiation conditions at IVEM for subsequent atom probe tomography (APT) analysis.

intervention.description: Mechanical properties assessment

structure.description: irradiated layer

outcome.measurement_method: Keysight G200 Nanoindenter with a diamond, pyramidal (Berkovich) tip

evidence_spans: Nanoindentation tests were performed on the as-deposited and post-irradiated materials using a Keysight G200 Nanoindenter with a diamond, pyramidal (Berkovich) tip to a final displacement of 1000 nm with a constant strain rate (loading rate divided by the load) of 0.05 s −1 . Continuous stiffness measurements (CSM) were performed at a frequency of 45 Hz and 2 nm displacement amplitude. Since the irradiated layer is 200–300 nm and size effect can be around three times the indented depth (for brittle materials), the hardness and modulus measurements were obtained at 200 nm indentation depth.

intervention.description: Irradiated with 1-MeV Kr +2 and 16 keV He +

structure.description: irradiation-induced damage state

conditions.environment: in situ TEM at IVEM-Tandem Facility

evidence_spans: In the dual-beam ion irradiations, the material was irradiated to 8.5 displacements per atom (dpa) and ~9% He. The implanted He per dpa ratio was ~1.07% He/dpa. The corresponding Kr and He fluences were 2.74 × 10 15 and 5.84 × 10 16 ions/cm 2 with average fluxes of 4.86 × 10 11 and 1.04 × 10 13 ions/cm 2 /s, respectively. The irradiation temperature in both dual and single-beam irradiation experiments was set to 1173 K. In situ videos were collected for irradiation-induced damage quantification. The damage quantification procedure is well described in ref. [60] . For bubble density determination, random arrays of 15 nm circles were drawn on each grain using ImageJ software [61] and bubbles are counted in every circle and divided by the area of the circle. An average is taken as the bubble density. For bubble area determination, ImageJ software was used to draw a circle around the perimeters of the bubbles on every grain. The areas of the circles are determined, and an average is taken.
The overall change in volume after irradiation was calculated using Δ v / v = 4 3 π r c 3 N v where N v is the bubble density in a 100 nm thick foil and r c is the radius of the bubble.
